extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in number theory; general readers interested in mathematical conjectures
extracted.subtask_description: Page describes the Pólya conjecture: its statement in elementary terms, an equivalent formulation via the summatory Liouville function, definitions of the functions involved, its disproof, and explicit counterexamples and numerical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya conjecture (odd prime-factors majority formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n > 1, if the natural numbers ≤ n are partitioned into those with an odd number of prime factors and those with an even number of prime factors, then the former set has at least as many members as the latter set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated prime factors are counted repeatedly; e.g., 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 has an odd number of prime factors, while 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 has an even number. The informal meaning given is that 'most' (i.e., 50% or more) of the natural numbers ≤ n have an odd number of prime factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent formulation using the summatory Liouville function
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjecture is equivalently that L(n) = ∑_{k=1}^{n} λ(k) ≤ 0 for all n > 1, where λ(k) = (-1)^{Ω(k)} and Ω(k) counts the total number of prime factors of k (with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reformulation makes the conjecture a sign/partial-sum statement about the Liouville function. It ties the parity of prime-factor counts to cumulative sums: λ(k) is positive when Ω(k) is even and negative when Ω(k) is odd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of λ(k) and Ω(k)
rubrics_metrics.description: λ(k) = (-1)^{Ω(k)}, where Ω(k) counts the total number of prime factors of k (counted with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, λ(k) is positive if the number of prime factors of k is even, and negative if it is odd. This definition underpins both the combinatorial 'odd/even prime factors' statement and the summatory Liouville function formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof / existence of counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pólya conjecture is false: C. Brian Haselgrove (1958) showed the conjecture has a counterexample (he estimated it to be around 1.845 × 10^{361}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit much smaller counterexamples were later produced: R. Sherman Lehman (1960) gave n = 906,180,359; Minoru Tanaka (1980) found the smallest counterexample n = 906,150,257. The conjecture fails for most n in the region 906,150,257 ≤ n ≤ 906,488,079, and in that region the summatory Liouville function reaches a maximum value of 829 at n = 906,316,571.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/interpretive note about Pólya's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Although commonly called the Pólya conjecture, Pólya himself did not assert the statement as true; he showed that the truth of the statement would imply the Riemann hypothesis, so it is more accurately described as 'Pólya's problem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies historical attribution and connects the statement to broader conjectures (Riemann hypothesis) rather than claiming Pólya actually conjectured its truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative lesson: size of smallest counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparatively large size (though not astronomically large) of the smallest counterexample is used to illustrate that a conjecture can hold for many initial cases yet fail in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites this as an example of the 'strong law of small numbers'—small-sample observations can be misleading about global truth.
